title: How do you ship a game in e.g. 6 weeks? My specs alone take days
author: castor44_
selftext:
I keep seeing posts like "made a game in 6 weeks with AI". I'm genuinely curious how. I'm building a colony sim in Godot, working with an LLM. For ONE milestone (just a slice of the game), I spend 2–3 evenings ONLY on the spec. So no code yet.

The typing ofc isn't the slow part. It's the decisions: what happens when X? What if Y runs out? How do systems interact? etc

So I wonder: do you spec less and fix things as you go? Are those "6-week games" much smaller in scope?

Or am I just overthinking it? How does your workflow look?

comments.author: geddy
comments.body:
My theory is, the more experience you have as a) someone who plays video games, and b) a real actual software engineer with years of experience, directly dictates the how long it takes you to make a game of any size. If you've been playing video games for decades, you know what makes them fun and what makes them suck. If you're an engineer, you know what to test for, spend more time on polish, cleaning up the codebase, etc.

Unless you're making Pong or Hangman, 6 weeks for a game of even reasonable complexity is ridiculously short. There just isn't enough time in that span to even sufficiently *play test* your game, let alone find all the tiny little bits that need polish.

Heck I spend most of my time playing the game, writing down every teeny tiny thing that looks even slightly off, anything that annoys me, any friction whatsoever, because I know from playing games for over 35 years the things that make a game look shitty. And more importantly, the little touches that I *look* for myself.

I mean I just spent 3 days tweaking my user interface on different screens, standardizing it all into separate components because I realized it was too button-happy. Problem with being an engineer is you tend to end up designing like an engineer lol, so I have to tap into my decades of UX/UI experience as well.

NOW - my point is, remove the engineering experience, the UX/UI experience, the gaming experience even, and yes, you can probably ship a great big pile of shit that no one will ever play in 6 weeks.

replies.author: metalblessing

100%. When I made my first game (in hindsight a roguelike bullethell was probably not the best choice for a first game). 600 weapons and clothing pieces. It’s a pretty important part of my loop though since the part I find the most fun is just finding the items,  going to the item rooms and hopefully getting lucky and finding good synergies. But there is a challenge in not having to many boring items and also making special items feel special. My game prolly doesn’t look very good right now but all my items are my favorite part personally and a lot of the unlocks and progress is based on item collection plus most of my items pedestals for the first two levels draw from a “T1” tagged item pool which o don’t intend to use for the 3rd and 4th floor since the setting will change so much (more fantasy based items) so I need to fill out the other catagories and some other rooms use more unique tags I need to fill out (like one of my trailor interiors is an AA meeting which pulls items with an alcohol tag, there are also consumables) so my idea needed a lot. It’s essentially meant to be 3 item pools though for 3 parts of the game. Also all player enemies and NPCs use the created assets so it helps add variety when enemies can be dressed a large variety of ways. But there is a problem with having to many assets where I have to make time to test and inspect all of them unless they are literally just a recolor or logo added to an existing assets where but even then the stats and value has to make sense for the rarity.

replies.author: duskaception
replies.body: One thing that's really sped up my iterations is having a built in "bug report" feature, reads all the metadeta of where im looking, location, current quest data, yada yada, then I just tell it to read all my "marks" and it goes through one by one, sorts by what to tackle first then gets to work. Test again, repeat, set up a couple agents to run through the game itself to look for bugs, have it work on building specific tools to find issues with different things like gameplay balance, visual fidelity, collision issues. Just really have it build a suite of tools for you and itself to efficiently test things. All of that really speeds up things. Other than that having a clear vision on the style and story of your game makes things go a million times faster with rough drafting and then polishing.

comments.author: CycleMother2006
comments.body:
I wouldn't  be speccing out every single feature before you have code in place, unless these are very broad, unrefined ideas. Otherwise I guarantee you're going to find yourself rewriting most of them anyway when it comes time to implement, because other changes that were mandated for performance reasons or compatibility or feasibility or whatever will end up driving wedges in future features that you have to adapt for, and then the required changes in those will drive further deviations later, etc.

As for those posts, every one I've seen has been slop. There's maybe one or two exceptions which were very simple ideas to implement but had original core loops to them (8-man pong comes to mind) where you could implement them in a polished way in two months, but even then that timeline would be cutting it close simply because bug/QOL testing alone can take quite a while.

Most of the games with store links posted in this sub have been shameless advertisements by people dumping slop on the community in an effort to try and make a quick buck. In fact, the only time I really get critical of a game's apparent quality/polish is if they're trying to sell the game, in which case it should be deservedly put through the ringer to determine if it's ready to call itself a finished product.

comments.author: Economy_Bedroom3902
comments.body:
Colony sims are a LOT more work than the average game which ships in 6 weeks.  Most of them are either a reimagining of one of the low effort multi attempt games (flappy bird, subway surfer, etc), or a "1 main thing" game (the recent needle in a haystack and digging holes games)

Even before AI, the general platform is that you already have a template game where you have a character which can run around, jump, etc in one of the major engines.  And you've got a standard control scheme.  Everything you do you start from there so you aren't reinventing the wheel.  From there you just pick a small vertical slice and build it.

Most of the enterprises doing this type of thing aim to get like 5 games out per year, and they frequently change the name of the studio and orphan every old past game which doesn't do well.  They're aiming for lucky wins, and they don't want to get dragged into long expensive game dev projects.

AI has opened the door to accelerating the low effort slop, and rushing stolen ideas.  Where as it used to take ages to copy a complex, deep game, you can now basically just give the game to a fable agent and say "make me a clone of this game in unity" or whatever.  Then the job becomes the fastest possible reskin.

The really gross thing is that, because these studios are optimizing for quick wins, they often have a better sense for marketing sparkle and "friendly" game design.  They can make the more attractive, slightly more fun version of someone else's game faster than that someone else can figure out what additional polish they need, as the real game dev is planning for a multi year dev cycle, where as the cloner is trying just to catch the hype peak and discard the left over bones.

comments.author: aura-32
comments.body:
You're not overthinking it, a colony sim is just a different kind of game from most of those 6-week posts. Systems that feed each other (food, jobs, moods, resources) are exactly where the decisions you're describing live, and no amount of typing speed removes them.

One thing that can make the spec stage faster: only spec the questions that would be expensive to change later, like data shapes and how systems talk to each other, and leave tuning questions ("what if Y runs out") as open notes. Build the slice with placeholder answers, watch it run for a while, and you'll often find the sim answers half of those questions for you. Then write the spec for what you saw, not what you guessed.

comments.author: fhtiek
comments.body:
I think the short timescales are because they are making key concessions on scope, original content, and playtesting/iteration.

Like if you decided you are making a 10-level retro platformer inspired by super mario world, using low poly visuals and copying the style, and are not bothering to play and fine tune each level, you can probably do that in a week. Maybe even less.

The made in a weekend stuff i tend to see here very heavily borrowS mechanics, art style, and structure from something else. Meaning the dev gets to skip that work and theres no real spec to write, the model can do it since its working backwards from a known result. 

I suspect too theres a lack of iterative inprovement "find the fun" loops as well. Every good dev log Ive ever watched has been littered with a dev finishing a feature then realizing its not fun. They then go through this long loop of playtesting where the find the sauce and make it fun. I would guess this is most often skipped in these quick flip games, and would hazard a guess many of them arent very good as a result
